src: Great migrations: routes and timing from tracking studies and wildlife agencies (USFWS, USGS, NOAA Fisheries, NPS, USDA Forest Service, Parks Australia, DFO Canada, UNESCO, NASA, CMS, BTO, Cornell Lab, Hawk Mountain, peer-reviewed papers).

mig.sp: Blue (white-bearded) wildebeest, plains zebra, Thomson's gazelle
p: Calving: about 8,000 calves a day for 4–6 weeks
Heading south as the short rains begin
Back on the southern plains by November
mig.km: about 1,000 km loop
mig.num: about 1.5–2 million wildebeest, about 300,000 zebra and 900,000 Thomson's gazelle
mig.f: The largest unaltered animal migration left on Earth, a clockwise loop across Tanzania and Kenya. Each February hundreds of thousands of calves are born on the southern plains within a few weeks.
mig.s: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; NASA

p: Wintering in the Ogilvie Mountains, Yukon
Cows head north from late March
Calving on the Arctic coastal plain, early June
Post-calving herds on the coastal plain
Richardson Mountains and Old Crow Flats
West into Alaska: Chandalar and Coleen rivers
mig.km: pregnant cows walk about 720 km each spring to the calving grounds
mig.num: about 218,000 in 2017; about 143,000 in the 2025 photo census
mig.f: The herd ranges over about 340,000 km² of mostly roadless Alaska and Yukon. Its cows calve on the Arctic coastal plain in early June, where there are few predators and good food.
mig.s: USFWS; Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game; Government of Yukon

p: Nxai Pan National Park, Botswana (wet season)
mig.km: about 250 km each way, 500 km round trip
mig.f: GPS-collared zebras revealed the longest recorded land migration in Africa. They crossed the Chobe River and walked due south to Nxai Pan in December of both 2012 and 2013.
mig.s: Naidoo et al. 2014 (Oryx)

p: Winter in the southern Betpak-Dala desert
Calving in the northern range, early May
mig.km: about 250 km a year on average; some travel more than 500 km
mig.f: These saiga move north and south with the seasons across the Kazakh steppe. Poaching and a 2015 disease die-off nearly wiped them out, but they have rebounded to more than a million.
mig.s: CMS (UN Convention on Migratory Species); Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative

p: Wintering in the Upper Green River Basin
Summer at the foot of the Tetons, Grand Teton NP
mig.km: up to about 240 km
mig.f: Pronghorn have used this corridor for at least 6,000 years. In 2008 it became the first federally designated wildlife migration corridor in the United States.
mig.s: NPS (Grand Teton); Wildlife Conservation Society; US Forest Service

mig.n: Red Desert to Hoback mule deer migration
p: Winter range in the Red Desert
North past the Wind River Range foothills
Summer on the slopes around the Hoback Basin
mig.km: about 240 km each way, 480 km round trip
mig.f: GPS collars revealed this route, announced in 2014 as the longest mule deer migration ever recorded. The deer spend about four months of every year on the move.
mig.s: University of Wyoming; Wyoming Migration Initiative

p: Last bats leave Kasanka NP, Zambia
Peak: the roost fills a few hectares of swamp forest
mig.km: the species travels up to about 2,000 km a year
mig.num: up to 10 million often cited; a 2019 camera count found about 0.75–1 million a night
mig.f: Every October to December, huge numbers of fruit bats crowd into a small patch of forest in Kasanka National Park. By weight it is the largest gathering of bats in the world.
mig.s: Koger et al. 2023 (Ecosphere); Max Planck Society; University of Konstanz

mig.sp: White-eared kob, tiang, Mongalla gazelle, Bohor reedbuck
p: Dry season: north and east toward Gambella, Ethiopia
Herds gather in Badingilo to breed in the wet season
After breeding, north and east toward Boma
mig.f: An aerial survey in 2023 counted about six million antelope moving across South Sudan's Boma–Badingilo landscape, which would make it the largest land-mammal migration on Earth.
mig.s: African Parks; Government of South Sudan

p: Overwintering in oyamel fir forests, central Mexico
mig.km: up to about 4,800 km
mig.f: The monarchs that fly south are the great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico in spring, yet they find the same few mountain forests. They overwinter there from about October to late March.
mig.s: USDA Forest Service; USFWS

p: Overwintering groves on the California coast
Disperse inland in early spring and breed
Summer generations spread across the West
The autumn generation heads to the coast
mig.km: about 480–1,600 km
mig.num: about 12,260 counted at 249 sites (2025); millions in the 1980s
mig.f: Western monarchs cluster in eucalyptus, Monterey pine and cypress groves along the California coast. Their numbers have fallen from millions in the 1980s to a few thousand.
mig.s: USFWS; Xerces Society Western Monarch Count

p: Winter breeding in the African savanna
mig.km: about 12,000–14,000 km round trip over several generations
mig.f: Over several generations painted ladies make the longest known insect migration, crossing the Sahara twice a year. Spring arrivals in the Mediterranean are the offspring of butterflies that flew south the autumn before.
mig.s: Talavera et al. 2018 (Biology Letters); Hu et al. 2021 (PNAS)

p: East Africa, breeding in rain pools
Some return through the Maldives in May
mig.km: an estimated 14,000–18,000 km circuit over generations, with at least 3,500 km of open ocean
mig.f: Millions of these dragonflies reach the Maldives each autumn, though the islands have no fresh water to breed in. They ride monsoon winds more than 1 km up to cross the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa.
mig.s: Anderson 2009 (Journal of Tropical Ecology); Hobson et al. 2012 (PLoS ONE)

p: Resting in alpine caves of the Australian Alps
Flying northwest across New South Wales
Breeding grounds on the inland plains
Arrive at cool caves above about 1,800 m
mig.km: up to about 1,000 km each way
mig.num: historically up to about 2 billion in the caves
mig.f: Bogong moths fly up to 1,000 km at night to the same alpine caves, packing up to 17,000 per square metre of rock. They steer by the Earth's magnetic field and the starry sky, the first insects shown to use the stars as a compass.
mig.s: Warrant et al. 2016 (Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience); Dreyer et al. 2025 (Nature)

p: The first heavy wet-season rain starts the march
Crossing roads and the town to the coast
Spawning before dawn on a falling high tide in the moon's last quarter
Baby crabs return to the forest about a month later
mig.num: tens of millions; recent official estimates exceed 100 million
mig.f: Huge numbers of red crabs march from the forest to the sea at the start of the wet season, timed to the moon, and each female releases up to 100,000 eggs into the ocean. Rangers close roads and build crab bridges to let them through.
mig.s: Parks Australia; DCCEEW (Australian Government)

p: Leaves the Southern Ocean in April
Back at the colony in northeast Greenland
The route splits off West Africa
Reaches the Weddell Sea in late November
mig.km: about 70,900 km round trip on average
mig.f: Tracked Arctic terns from Greenland and Iceland flew about 70,900 km a year, the longest annual migration recorded for any animal. Heading south some follow the African coast and others cross to follow Brazil's.
mig.s: Egevang et al. 2010 (PNAS)

p: Leaves the Yellow Sea for Alaska
Nonstop across the Pacific to New Zealand
mig.km: about 11,700 km nonstop south; record 13,560 km in 11 days (2022)
mig.f: Bar-tailed godwits fly nonstop across the Pacific from Alaska to New Zealand and Australia. In 2022 a 5-month-old bird flew a record 13,560 km in 11 days from Alaska to Tasmania.
mig.s: Gill et al. 2009 (Proc. R. Soc. B, USGS); BirdLife Australia

p: Breeding on Whenua Hou (Codfish Island), New Zealand
Leaves in late April to early May
Back at the colony in October
mig.km: about 64,000 km round trip
mig.f: Shearwaters tagged in New Zealand flew giant figure-eight loops across the Pacific, each to one feeding area off Japan, Alaska or California.
mig.s: Shaffer et al. 2006 (PNAS); UC Santa Cruz; NIWA

p: Strait of Gibraltar: 14 km of sea
mig.km: the sea crossing at Gibraltar is only about 14 km
mig.num: more than 100,000 storks pass Gibraltar each year
mig.f: Storks avoid long sea crossings, so western European birds funnel through the Strait of Gibraltar. Many now stop short: of tracked German and Austrian young storks, about 55% wintered in Spain and Portugal.
mig.s: Cheng et al. 2019 (Ecology and Evolution); Scientific Reports 2020

mig.km: about 4,400–4,600 km to northern Sudan, farther for birds going on
mig.f: Satellite-tracked storks from Germany and Poland crossed the Bosphorus, passed the Jordan Valley and followed the Nile, reaching northern Sudan in about 20 days. Some later moved on to East or southern Africa.
mig.s: Satellite tracking of white storks, International Ornithological Congress proceedings

p: Reaches Britain, on average about 4 April
mig.km: about 9,700 km each way
mig.f: Many British swallows winter in South Africa, crossing the Sahara both ways. A swallow ringed in Staffordshire was caught in Natal in December 1912.
mig.s: British Trust for Ornithology

p: Lands on the US Gulf coast after 18–20 hours
Passes the Gulf coast in September
mig.km: about 800 km nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico
mig.f: In spring a ruby-throated hummingbird nearly doubles its weight, from about 3.25 g to 6 g, then flies about 800 km nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico in 18–20 hours.
mig.s: National Park Service; Cornell Lab of Ornithology

p: Breeding as far as Alaska and eastern Siberia
mig.num: hundreds of thousands stage on the Platte each spring (USFWS counts)
mig.f: Mid-continent sandhill cranes winter from Texas and New Mexico into Mexico and breed across Arctic Canada, Alaska and eastern Siberia. In spring most stop on Nebraska's Platte River.
mig.s: USFWS

p: Crosses the Himalayas in one day
Breeding at mountain lakes in Mongolia
mig.km: the Himalayan crossing takes a single day
mig.f: Bar-headed geese cross the Himalayas between India and Central Asia. They climb 4,000–6,000 m in 7–8 hours, the fastest sustained climbs recorded for any bird.
mig.s: Hawkes et al. 2011 (PNAS, USGS)

p: Breeding in Mongolia and northeast China
Across the Indian Ocean to Africa
mig.km: about 12,900 km each way
mig.num: the Nagaland roost is estimated at about one million birds
mig.f: Amur falcons pause in Nagaland, India, in late October to feast on termites. Then they fly about 4,000 km across the Indian Ocean in 4–5 days, the longest sea crossing of any bird of prey.
mig.s: Cornell Lab of Ornithology; CMS

p: Delaware Bay: horseshoe crab eggs in May
Nearly doubles its weight in two weeks
mig.km: up to about 15,000 km each way
mig.f: Rufa red knots fly up to 15,000 km each way between South America and the Canadian Arctic. Delaware Bay is the last spring stop for 50–80% of them, where horseshoe crab eggs let them nearly double their weight.
mig.s: USFWS

mig.km: about 14,500 km each way
mig.f: Wheatears that breed in Alaska weigh about 25 g yet fly about 14,500 km each way, across Siberia and Arabia, to winter in eastern Africa.
mig.s: Bairlein et al. 2012 (Biology Letters)

mig.sp: Swainson's hawk, with broad-winged hawks, turkey vultures and Mississippi kites
p: The River of Raptors over Veracruz
Over the Andes to central Argentina
mig.km: about 13,500 km south, 12,000 km north (tracked Swainson's hawks)
mig.num: about 4.5 million raptors counted each autumn at Veracruz
mig.f: Raptors funnel between the mountains and the Gulf of Mexico at Veracruz, where counters log about 4.5 million each autumn, including about 90% of the world's Swainson's hawks.
mig.s: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary; Fuller et al. 1998 (USGS); Kochert et al. 2011 (Condor)

p: Wintering in the Congo basin rainforest
Refuels in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana
Reaches Britain, on average about 19 April
Across the Sahara to the Congo basin
mig.km: about 16,000 km round trip
mig.f: Satellite tracking showed British cuckoos all winter in the Congo basin. They return via West Africa, crossing the Sahara in one nonstop flight of about 3,000 km.
mig.s: BTO Cuckoo Tracking Project

p: South of the Antarctic Polar Front
mig.f: Tracked short-tailed shearwaters first fly south of the Antarctic Polar Front, then race north to spend the northern summer off Japan or in the Bering Sea, returning through the central Pacific in a loop.
mig.s: Carey et al. 2014 (Emu)

mig.f: Snow geese from Russia's Wrangel Island winter in two groups: most around the Fraser and Skagit deltas of British Columbia and Washington, the rest in California's Central Valley.
mig.s: USGS

p: Baja California lagoons: calves born January–February
North past the US West Coast
Summer feeding in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
mig.km: about 16,000–19,000 km round trip; some over 22,000 km
mig.f: Gray whales feed all summer in the Arctic, then swim to Mexico's Baja California lagoons, where calves are born. It is among the longest migrations of any mammal.
mig.s: NOAA Fisheries

mig.km: about 4,800 km each way, in as little as 28 days
mig.num: about half of all North Pacific humpbacks winter in Hawaiʻi
mig.f: Some humpbacks swim the 4,800 km between Alaska and Hawaiʻi in as little as 28 days. They feed in Alaska and give birth in warm Hawaiian waters.
mig.s: NOAA Fisheries; Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary

mig.km: about 8,300 km each way
mig.f: Whales photographed feeding in Antarctica were matched to Costa Rica, about 8,300 km away, then the longest documented movement of any mammal.
mig.s: Rasmussen et al. 2007 (Biology Letters); Modest et al. 2021 (Animal Biotelemetry)

p: Feeding on jellyfish off central California
mig.km: more than 10,000 km each way
mig.f: Leatherbacks that nest in Papua, Indonesia, cross the Pacific to eat jellyfish off California, a trip of more than 10,000 km that takes 10–12 months.
mig.s: Benson et al. 2011 (Ecosphere); NOAA Fisheries

mig.km: nearly 13,000 km across the Pacific
mig.f: North Pacific loggerheads hatch in Japan, then drift and swim nearly 13,000 km to feed off Baja California, Mexico, where they stay for decades before returning to nest.
mig.s: NOAA Fisheries

mig.km: more than 2,200 km each way
mig.f: Green turtles that nest on tiny Ascension Island, in the middle of the South Atlantic, feed off Brazil more than 2,200 km away, and find the island again to nest.
mig.s: Hays et al. 2001 (Journal of Experimental Biology)

mig.n: European eel to the Sargasso Sea
mig.km: more than 5,000 km from Europe
mig.f: Adult European eels leave Europe's rivers in autumn and swim more than 5,000 km to spawn in the Sargasso Sea. In 2022 a tagged eel gave the first direct evidence of an adult reaching the breeding area.
mig.s: Righton et al. 2016 (Science Advances); Wright et al. 2022 (Scientific Reports)

p: Enter the Yukon River mouth in mid-May
Whitehorse fish ladder; spawning in late summer
mig.km: about 2,000 km upstream just to reach Canada; the river is over 3,000 km long
mig.f: Chinook salmon bound for Canada enter the Yukon River in May and reach the border about two months later. Some swim all the way to Whitehorse, where they climb a fish ladder in July and August.
mig.s: Fisheries and Oceans Canada; Government of Yukon

p: Spawning in the Gulf of Mexico, April–June
Out to the central and eastern Atlantic
mig.f: Western Atlantic bluefin tuna spawn in the Gulf of Mexico in spring, then cross to feeding grounds in the central and eastern Atlantic, where they mix with fish from the Mediterranean. They can reach 4 m and 900 kg.
mig.s: Block et al. 2005 (Nature); NOAA Fisheries

mig.num: about 219 adult and sub-adult sharks off central California
mig.f: White sharks hunt seals off central California each autumn, then travel to a remote patch of ocean halfway to Hawaiʻi, nicknamed the White Shark Café, where they stay for months. They return to the same coastal hotspots year after year.
mig.s: Jorgensen et al. 2010 (Proc. R. Soc. B); NOAA Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary

mig.f: Each winter sardines move north along South Africa's east coast, drawing dolphins, sharks and seabirds. Records since 1946 show the run now reaches Durban about 1.3 days later each decade as the sea warms.
mig.s: Coetzee et al. 2010 (African Journal of Marine Science); Fitchett & Grab 2019 (South African Journal of Science)

p: Año Nuevo: breeding on the beach
Back on land to molt in June
mig.km: at least 21,000 km a year (males), 18,000 km (females)
mig.f: Northern elephant seals go to sea twice a year, after breeding and after molting. Males feed as far as the western Aleutians, up to 4,775 km away, and spend about 250 days a year at sea.
mig.s: Stewart & DeLong 1995 (Journal of Mammalogy); Le Boeuf et al. 2000 (Ecological Monographs)

p: Offshore in the eastern Indian Ocean
mig.km: some tracked sharks went about 3,500 km, to the Gulf of Carpentaria
mig.f: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia has one of the world's largest known gatherings of whale sharks, mostly young males. Tags show some travel to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and the Gulf of Carpentaria, diving as deep as 1,906 m.
mig.s: Bignell et al. 2025 (Marine Biology); CSIRO

p: Summer feeding near the South Orkney Islands
Spring feeding on the Patagonian Shelf
mig.f: Whales tagged off the Falkland Islands in 2022 moved on to Península Valdés, Argentina, then fed on the Patagonian Shelf in spring. Some males went on to the Scotia Sea and the Antarctic Peninsula.
mig.s: Weir et al. 2024 (Endangered Species Research)

p: Winter breeding in Bering Sea pack ice
mig.f: Most Pacific walruses, especially females and calves, follow the sea ice north through the Bering Strait in spring. As summer ice retreats, more of them now rest on coastal beaches.
mig.s: USFWS; USGS

mig.n: Blue whales to the Costa Rica Dome
p: Summer and autumn feeding off California
mig.km: tracked whales averaged 5,430 km
mig.f: Blue whales tagged off California head south in winter to Baja California and the Costa Rica Dome, a cool upwelling patch of the tropical Pacific, feeding along the way, and return around June.
mig.s: Bailey et al. 2009 (Endangered Species Research)
